summary: When a DNS query is redirected by a CNAME or DNAME, the answer can involve several lookup rounds. This RFC clarifies how the response code (RCODE) and status bits in the final answer relate to the first lookup and to the later ones. It updates RFC 1035, RFC 2308 and RFC 2672.

eli5.summary: If you ask for a person and get pointed to a new address, the final note should say how the whole trip went. This RFC says which part of the trip the answer's status describes.

dns response code after cname chain
what does rcode mean in dns
subtitle: Clarifies how response codes and status bits work when DNS names are redirected

tldr.problem: DNS queries can be redirected through CNAME or DNAME records, creating multiple lookup rounds. The original specifications were unclear about how response codes and status bits should be set in these cases.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC clarifies that the response code should be set based on the final lookup cycle, while status bits like the Authoritative Answer and Authentic Data bits follow specific rules based on which part of the chain they refer to.
tldr.outcome: DNS implementations now have clear, consistent rules for handling redirected queries, reducing interoperability problems.

today: RFC 6604 updates the DNS specifications to clarify behavior with name redirection. It works with RFC 1035 (the original DNS spec), RFC 2308 (negative caching), and RFC 2672 (DNAME).

sections.title: Name Redirection in DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) uses CNAME (Canonical Name) and DNAME records to redirect queries to different names. When a query for one name encounters a CNAME or DNAME, the resolver gets redirected and must perform a new lookup.

Multiple redirections can form a chain: name A points to name B, which points to name C, and so on. The difficulty is that a DNS response header includes a response code (RCODE) to indicate errors, and status bits to indicate whether the answer is authoritative and authentic. When redirection happens, these fields become ambiguous: do they refer to the first lookup, the final lookup, or something in between?
sections.eli5: Imagine following directions: "Go to house 5, but that's not the real place—go to house 10 instead." The response needs to say whether you reached the right house, not whether house 5 was the right address.

sections.title: Setting the Response Code
sections.content:
This RFC clarifies that when an xNAME chain is followed, the response code must be set based on the final lookup cycle, not the initial one. If the chain encounters an error during the final lookup, the RCODE reflects that error. If the final lookup succeeds, the RCODE is set to zero.

Since intermediate lookups in a chain necessarily succeed before redirection occurs, the error information from those intermediate steps is not carried forward. Only the result of the final lookup matters for the response code.
sections.eli5: Only the last address you try to reach matters for the final error code, not the ones you were pointed through along the way.

sections.title: Status Bits
sections.content:
The Authoritative Answer (AA) bit indicates whether the answer is from a server authoritative for that zone. For xNAME chains, the AA bit is set based on the first answer in the chain.

The Authentic Data (AD) bit, used with DNSSEC security, indicates that the response is authentic. According to DNSSEC rules, the AD bit can only be set if all data returned in both the answer and authority sections is authentic. For xNAME chains, this applies to all the data across the entire chain.
sections.eli5: The AA bit says whether the server knows about the first name you asked about. The AD bit says whether the entire chain of answers is secure and trusted.
